headline: Congolese NGO Takes Historic Lead in Managing Protected Area
meta_description: For the first time, a Congolese organization will co-manage a major protected area, centering local communities in conservation efforts.
summary_short: Strong Roots becomes the first Congolese NGO to co-manage a protected area in DRC history, bringing community-centered conservation to Itombwe Nature Reserve.
body:
In a historic shift for conservation in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the NGO Strong Roots has been entrusted with co-managing Itombwe Nature Reserve, a 760,000-hectare protected area in South Kivu province. Under a 10-year public-private partnership with the Congolese Wildlife Authority, Strong Roots will become the first Congolese organization to lead management of a major protected area in the country's modern history. The reserve is home to nearly 600 bird species and serves as a sanctuary for critically endangered Grauer's gorillas. Dominique Bikaba, Strong Roots' founder, emphasized that the government selected his organization because of its decade-long work building trust with local communities—an approach that stands in sharp contrast to the DRC's conservation history.

Most protected areas in the DRC were created by evicting Indigenous populations, fueling decades of conflict between park authorities and residents. Strong Roots offers a different model. Over the past ten years, the organization has secured 23 community forest concessions covering nearly 600,000 hectares, creating a wildlife and community corridor between Kahuzi-Biega National Park and Itombwe. Bikaba, himself from an Indigenous community displaced by a previous protected area, is determined to center local populations in conservation rather than exclude them.

The organization plans to recruit community members as patrol staff and combine traditional and modern conservation methods. Bikaba stated that by working alongside residents, Strong Roots aims to reduce wildlife decline while making communities less vulnerable to recruitment by armed groups active in the region. The approach also prioritizes demilitarizing enforcement, stepping away from armed park rangers toward collaborative law enforcement against poaching and illegal mining. For the first time, the DRC's conservation future rests in Congolese hands.
